1. Executive Summary and Scope

This report delivers a legal, technical, and financial audit of the research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework, innovation grant architecture, administrative compliance procedures, and judicial jurisprudence of Canada as of November 2026.

Canada operates a comprehensive R&D fiscal support system, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under Section 37, Section 127, Section 127.1, and Subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Between December 2024 and November 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential legislative transformation since 2012. Enacted via Bill C-15 (which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026) following the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) and Budget 2025, the federal government doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million, expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average revenue phase-out test, and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, equipment lease costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) for property acquired after December 15, 2024.

Simultaneously, Budget 2026 proposed a $930 million five-year commercialization expansion to bring regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs (for patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software) into the SR&ED regime for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026. At the administrative level, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process in April 2026 using Form T1322, offering businesses with under $25 million in gross revenue upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cutting post-filing expenditure review processing times in half from 180 days to 90 days. At the provincial level, Québec enacted the landmark Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) in its 2025–2026 Budget for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025—consolidating eight legacy R&D credits into a unified 30% / 20% refundable credit covering both R&D and pre-commercialization activities as well as capital equipment—while British Columbia (via Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) made its 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent and harmonized with the federal $6 million limit, ECPC access, and capital expenditure restoration, and Ontario automatically restored capital expenditure eligibility for both the 8% Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) and the 3.5% Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC).
2. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
2.1 Core Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The federal SR&ED program is not governed by a standalone innovation statute; rather, its legal authority is embedded within an interlocking set of provisions across the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), jointly structured by the Department of Finance Canada and administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). A rigorous audit of any Canadian R&D claim requires cross-referencing four primary statutory pillars.

The Definitional Pillar (Subsection 248(1) of the ITA) establishes the substantive legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" (SR&ED), dividing qualifying work into basic research (paragraph (a)), applied research (paragraph (b)), experimental development (paragraph (c)), and eight enumerated categories of directly supporting work (paragraph (d)), while explicitly carving out seven categories of excluded commercial, routine, or non-technological activities in paragraphs (e) through (k). Subsection 248(1) also defines "salary or wages" (income from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the ITA) and "specified employee" (an employee who has a significant equity interest—10% or more of the shares of any class—or does not deal at arm's length with the employer).

The Income Deduction Pillar (Section 37 of the ITA) governs the accumulation and deduction of allowable SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada through a perpetual tax pool known as the "pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures". Subsection 37(1) authorizes taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada to deduct current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and—following the post-December 15, 2024 restoration—capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer. Related subsections govern payments to related corporations actively engaged in business (subsection 37(1.1)), available-for-use timing rules for capital property (subsection 37(1.2)), SR&ED carried on in Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone (subsection 37(1.3)), the limit on permissible salary or wages for SR&ED performed outside Canada (subsection 37(1.5)), deductions for research outside Canada (subsection 37(2)), the prohibition on deducting expenditures made to acquire rights in or arising out of SR&ED (subsection 37(4)), deemed capital cost allowance (CCA) treatment for SR&ED capital expenditures (subsection 37(6)), loss restriction event rules upon an acquisition of control (subsection 37(6.1)), expenditure qualification rules under the traditional and proxy methods (subsection 37(8)), deemed corporate association rules for sharing the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) cap (subsection 37(9.5)), the irrevocable annual election to use the Prescribed Proxy Amount (subsection 37(10)), the mandatory 18-month prescribed form filing requirement (subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12)), and the look-through rule for third-party and contract payments (subsection 37(14)).

The Investment Tax Credit Pillar (Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA) governs tax credit calculation, application, and refundability. Subsection 127(5) permits taxpayers to deduct Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) from Part I tax otherwise payable, including carrybacks of up to three years and carryforwards of up to 20 years. Subsection 127(8) governs the allocation of ITCs earned by partnerships to their respective members. Subsection 127(9) contains the foundational definitions of "investment tax credit", "qualified expenditure", "government assistance", "non-government assistance", "contract payment", "super-allowance benefit amount", "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC), "consolidated financial statements", "first term shared-use-equipment", and "second term shared-use-equipment", as well as the mandatory 18-month filing deadline for ITC schedules (paragraphs 127(9)(m) and (m.1)). Subsections 127(10.1) through 127(10.64) govern the enhanced 20% ITC addition (yielding a combined 35% rate) and the calculation, allocation, and phase-out of the annual expenditure limit for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and ECPCs. Subsections 127(11.5) to 127(11.8) regulate adjustments to qualified expenditures and non-arm's length cost caps; subsections 127(13) to 127(15) regulate the transfer of qualified expenditures between non-arm's length parties via Form T1146; subsections 127(18) to 127(22) regulate reductions for assistance and contract payments and their allocation via Form T1145; subsection 127(26) establishes the 180-day unpaid amount rule for non-salary current expenditures; and subsections 127(27) to 127(36) enforce the 20-year ITC recapture regime. Finally, Section 127.1 (specifically subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01)) governs the calculation and payment of the "refundable investment tax credit".

The Regulatory Pillar (Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations, Sections 2900 to 2903) supplies the granular operational mechanics required by Sections 37 and 127 of the ITA. Subsection 2900(2) defines expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED under the traditional method (including paragraph 2900(2)(a) for materials consumed or transformed, paragraph 2900(2)(b) for directly engaged employee remuneration, and paragraph 2900(2)(c) for other expenditures directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED). Subsection 2900(3) defines expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED under the traditional method. Subsections 2900(4) through 2900(10) establish the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) formula, the salary base exclusions, the specified employee caps (75% of salary and 2.5 × YMPE), the overall PPA cap, and deemed corporate associations. Subsection 2900(11) defines "prescribed depreciable property" (PDP) excluded from Shared-Use Equipment eligibility. Section 2902 enumerates "prescribed expenditures" that are excluded from the definition of "qualified expenditure" for ITC purposes (such as legal and accounting fees, financing and interest expenses, scientific society membership dues, acquisitions of rights under paragraph 2902(c), and used equipment under paragraph 2902(b)). Section 2903 governs prescribed special-purpose buildings approved by the Department of Finance.

body.text: 2.2 The 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms: 2024 Fall Economic Statement, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15

Between 2014 and 2024, the federal SR&ED regime operated under constraints introduced in the 2012 Federal Budget: the basic ITC rate was fixed at 15%, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs were completely excluded for property acquired after December 31, 2013, the enhanced 35% refundable ITC was restricted exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) up to a $3 million annual expenditure limit, and that $3 million limit phased out over a prior-year taxable capital range of $10 million to $50 million. (Earlier, the 2019 Federal Budget had repealed the prior-year taxable income phase-out test from the federal CCPC expenditure limit calculation, leaving taxable capital employed in Canada as the sole phase-out metric for tax years prior to late 2024).

Following consultations by the Department of Finance, the federal government announced a comprehensive modernization of the SR&ED program in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled on December 16, 2024), refined the expenditure limit further in Budget 2025, and enacted the statutory amendments into law through Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Unless otherwise specified for property acquisition dates, these enacted legislative reforms apply to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024).

First, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit to $6 million. While the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed raising the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million, Budget 2025 increased the limit further to $6 million (an additional $293 million fiscal commitment over five years: $3 million in 2025–2026, $70 million in 2026–2027, $85 million in 2027–2028, $65 million in 2028–2029, and $70 million in 2029–2030). Under Bill C-15, eligible corporations can earn up to $2.1 million per year ($6,000,000 × 35%) in enhanced SR&ED ITCs on current expenditures, up from the previous $1.05 million ceiling.

Second, Bill C-15 expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10M–$50M to $15M–$75M. For CCPCs calculating their expenditure limit under the taxable capital method (subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA), the threshold at which the $6 million expenditure limit begins to phase out was increased from $10 million to $15 million of taxable capital employed in Canada in the immediately preceding taxation year (combined across all associated corporations), and the threshold at which the expenditure limit is completely eliminated was raised from $50 million to $75 million.

Third, Bill C-15 extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and introduced an optional revenue phase-out election for CCPCs. Amending subsection 127(10.1), subsection 127(9), subsection 127(10.6), and subsection 127.1(2.01) of the ITA, the legislation grants ECPCs access to the enhanced 35% ITC (100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures) on up to $6 million of qualified SR&ED expenditures per taxation year. An ECPC's $6 million expenditure limit phases out based on its average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (as reported in its consolidated financial statements) between $15 million and $75 million. Furthermore, under newly enacted subsections 127(10.31) (for a standalone CCPC) and 127(10.32) (for a CCPC with associated corporations), CCPCs may elect on a prescribed form to determine their $6 million expenditure limit phase-out using the three-year average annual revenue method ($15 million to $75 million range) instead of the prior-year taxable capital method. Where CCPCs are associated, all CCPCs in the associated group must jointly elect to use the revenue method, aggregating each member corporation's revenue over the preceding three fiscal years regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire period (with reasonable adjustments permitted for intra-group sales).

Fourth, Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, equipment lease costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE). The legislation restored paragraph 37(1)(b) of the ITA and amended subsections 37(6), 37(6.1), 37(8), 127(9), 127(11.5), 127.1(2), 127.1(2.01) of the ITA and paragraph 2902(b) of the ITR to reinstate the eligibility of depreciable capital property and equipment lease costs for both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 ITC. This restoration applies to depreciable property acquired (and available for use) on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024) and, in the case of lease costs, to amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. Both "all or substantially all" (ASA — 90% or more) capital property and first-term / second-term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — used primarily, i.e., more than 50% of operating time, for SR&ED) are once again eligible. Unused ITCs earned at the enhanced 35% rate on qualified SR&ED capital expenditures are 40% refundable for both CCPCs and ECPCs.
2.3 Budget 2026 Commercialization and Intellectual Property Protection Expansion

Building upon the Bill C-15 reforms, the federal government tabled Budget 2026, proposing a targeted expansion of the SR&ED program to bridge the gap between laboratory R&D and commercial market entry. With a projected federal fiscal cost of $930 million over five years ($25 million in 2026–2027, $200 million in 2027–2028, $245 million in 2028–2029, $225 million in 2029–2030, and $235 million in 2030–2031), the Budget 2026 measures apply to taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day 2026 and encompass two structural additions:

items: Regulatory and Certification Testing Activities: Under existing SR&ED rules (subsection 248(1)), once technological uncertainty is resolved, subsequent testing conducted solely to satisfy regulatory or statutory certification requirements was frequently disallowed as routine testing or quality control under paragraph 248(1)(f). Budget 2026 expands eligible SR&ED activities to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process. To qualify, these regulatory and certification activities must directly relate to an underlying project that is eligible under existing SR&ED rules. Claimants may claim the full suite of eligible SR&ED expenditure categories—including employee salaries and wages, materials, contracting costs, overhead costs, and machinery and equipment—for qualifying regulatory validation work.

Intellectual Property (IP) Protection and Maintenance Expenditures: Budget 2026 expands eligible SR&ED expenditures to cover costs related to the registration and maintenance of IP protection for intellectual property developed in the course of conducting an eligible SR&ED project. The four eligible forms of IP protection—whether registered under Canadian legislation or equivalent legislation in a foreign jurisdiction—are patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. Eligible IP expenditures include expenses reasonably incurred to prepare and file an application for an eligible form of IP protection, as well as periodic maintenance costs payable to keep the IP rights in force. Under the geographic nexus rules set out in Budget 2026, administrative fees paid directly to an IP office outside Canada are eligible, whereas costs for supporting professional activities (such as preparing an application) are eligible only if conducted in Canada. Litigation costs or other expenses incurred to enforce IP rights against alleged infringement, or costs not directly connected to securing and maintaining IP rights, remain strictly excluded. Furthermore, if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED support was provided in respect of IP protection costs, recapture rules will apply to claw back the related SR&ED deduction and investment tax credit amounts.

body.text: 3. Federal SR&ED Tax Incentives: Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryovers
3.1 The Dual-Incentive Mechanism: Section 37 Deduction Pool and Section 127 Investment Tax Credit

The federal SR&ED program operates through a sequential, two-stage tax benefit mechanism for corporations, individuals (sole proprietorships), trusts, and partnerships conducting eligible R&D in Canada.

In Stage 1 (The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under Subsection 37(1)), allowable current SR&ED expenditures (salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, 100% of arm's length and non-arm's length SR&ED contracts, third-party payments, post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs, and—if the traditional method is elected—overhead and other directly attributable expenditures) together with allowable post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital expenditures are pooled in Section C of Part 3 of Form T661. This pool is reduced by government and non-government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received by the filing due date (paragraph 37(1)(d)), provincial super-allowance benefits (paragraph 37(1)(d.1)), and SR&ED ITCs applied against tax payable or refunded in a preceding taxation year (paragraph 37(1)(e)). The resulting net pool balance (Line 455 of Form T661) may be deducted in full or in part in the current taxation year (Line 460) to reduce net income for tax purposes, or carried forward indefinitely (Line 470) to offset business income in any future taxation year.

In Stage 2 (The SR&ED Investment Tax Credit under Subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and Section 127.1), the claimant computes its "total qualified SR&ED expenditures" in Part 4 of Form T661 (Line 570) by taking total allowable expenditures (Line 400), adding the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502, if the proxy method was elected), adding first-term and second-term Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504, at 25% of capital cost per term), adding prior-year unpaid non-salary amounts paid in the year (Line 500), and adding qualified expenditures transferred from a non-arm's length performer via Form T1146 (Line 508), and then subtracting unpaid non-salary amounts at 180 days post-year-end (Line 520), 20% of arm's length contracts and third-party payments (Line 529, leaving 80% eligible), 100% of non-arm's length contracts (Line 541), prescribed expenditures such as used equipment (Lines 530/535), non-arm's length supplier cost adjustments (Line 542), and government/non-government assistance and contract payments (Lines 513–517 and Line 538). The resulting qualified SR&ED expenditures earn an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) claimed on Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals and trusts).

Crucially, because federal SR&ED ITCs applied or refunded in one taxation year reduce the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e) (or are included in income under paragraph 12(1)(v) and added back via paragraph 37(1)(c.1) if the pool balance becomes negative at year-end), the federal ITC is effectively taxed in the following taxation year. Exceptionally, because a partnership is not a separate person for income tax purposes and cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance (paragraph 96(1)(e.1)), a partnership must reduce its Section 37 pool by the SR&ED ITC earned in the same taxation year the expenditures are incurred and must deduct 100% of the remaining pool balance in computing partnership net income for that fiscal period.
3.2 Basic (15%) Versus Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates and Entity Qualification
The statutory rate at which a claimant earns SR&ED ITCs depends on the legal classification of the taxpayer and whether its qualified expenditures fall within its annual expenditure limit:

items: Basic ITC Rate (15%): Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the basic SR&ED ITC rate is 15%. The 15% basic rate applies to all corporations (other than CCPCs and ECPCs claiming within their expenditure limit), including foreign-controlled subsidiaries and large Canadian public or private corporations whose taxable capital or revenue exceeds the $75 million phase-out ceiling; qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a CCPC or an ECPC in excess of its annual expenditure limit for the taxation year; individuals (sole proprietors) and beneficiaries of trusts; and partners of a partnership (where under subsection 127(8), partnership ITCs are computed at the partnership level and allocated to partners, preventing corporate CCPC partners from earning the 35% enhanced rate on partnership SR&ED expenditures, as confirmed in All Colour Chemicals Ltd. v. The Queen).

Enhanced ITC Rate (35%): Under subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, an additional 20% ITC is added to the 15% basic rate, generating a combined enhanced ITC rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, only a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) (as defined in subsection 125(7) of the ITA—generally a private corporation resident in Canada that is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever [both de jure and de facto control], by one or more non-resident persons, one or more public corporations, or any combination thereof) qualified for the 35% rate. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the enhanced 35% rate applies to both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) throughout the taxation year.

body.text: 3.3 Expenditure Limit Calculations and Phase-Out Mechanics ($6 Million Cap and $15M–$75M Phase-Out)

The maximum pool of annual qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC is governed by subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.64) of the ITA. Both the historical formula (for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024) and the current enacted Bill C-15 formula (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) must be verified during multi-year tax audits.
A. Taxation Years Beginning Before December 16, 2024 (CCPCs Only — $3 Million Cap)

For taxation years beginning prior to December 16, 2024, only CCPCs qualified for the enhanced 35% rate, and the maximum annual expenditure limit was $3,000,000 (shared among associated CCPCs via Schedule T2SCH49). The expenditure limit was reduced on a straight-line basis when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and all associated corporations) reached $10,000,000, becoming nil at $50,000,000:

In this formula, A is nil ($0) if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $10,000,000 or less; otherwise, A is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000. Under this historical formula, every $100,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $10,000,000 reduced the $3,000,000 expenditure limit by $7,500 (a reduction rate of $0.075 per dollar of excess taxable capital).
B. Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024 (CCPCs and ECPCs — $6 Million Cap)

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit is $6,000,000 (shared across associated CCPCs or consolidated ECPC group members). The $6,000,000 limit phases out on a straight-line basis over a $60,000,000 range starting at $15,000,000 and becoming nil at $75,000,000:
In this formula, A is determined under one of two statutory methods:

items: Taxable Capital Method (Default for CCPCs under Subsection 127(10.2)): A is $0 if the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year is less than $15,000,000; otherwise, A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

Three-Year Average Annual Revenue Method (Mandatory for ECPCs under Subsection 127(10.6); Elective for CCPCs under Subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32)): A is $0 if the average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (from consolidated financial statements for ECPCs, or aggregated across all associated group members for electing CCPCs) is less than $15,000,000; otherwise, A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which average annual revenue over the preceding three fiscal years exceeds $15,000,000.

body.text: Under the post-December 15, 2024 formula, every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital (or three-year average annual revenue) above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $100,000 (a reduction rate of $0.10 per dollar of excess taxable capital or revenue): at $15,000,000 or less, the expenditure limit is $6,000,000 (maximum 35% ITC of $2,100,000); at $30,000,000, the expenditure limit is $4,500,000 (maximum 35% ITC of $1,575,000); at $45,000,000, the expenditure limit is $3,000,000 (maximum 35% ITC of $1,050,000); at $60,000,000, the expenditure limit is $1,500,000 (maximum 35% ITC of $525,000); and at $75,000,000 or greater, the expenditure limit is nil ($0), so all qualified expenditures earn the 15% basic ITC.
C. Short Taxation Years and Associated Group Allocations

If a corporation has a short taxation year (fewer than 365 days), its expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365 (for example, for a 184-day taxation year, $3,000,000 × [184 ÷ 365] = $1,512,328 under the legacy cap, or $6,000,000 × [184 ÷ 365] = $3,024,658 under the current $6 million cap). Furthermore, under subsection 127(10.5), specific rules apply when a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year. Associated CCPCs must file Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) to allocate the group expenditure limit; failure to file an agreement is governed by subsection 127(10.4).
3.4 Refundability Rules Across Claimant Categories (100% vs. 40% Refund Rates)

An SR&ED ITC must first be applied against the taxpayer's federal Part I income tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year under subsection 127(5). Any unclaimed balance of the ITC earned in the year may be refunded in cash under Section 127.1 (subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01)), depending on the claimant's legal status, whether the expenditures are within or above the expenditure limit, and whether the expenditures are of a current nature (including the PPA) or of a capital nature.

A critical distinction in Section 127.1 exists between a Qualifying Corporation, a Non-Qualifying CCPC, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC), and an Excluded Corporation. A Qualifying Corporation (subsection 127.1(2)) is a CCPC whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations) was not more than its Qualifying Income Limit for the current taxation year. Under the ITA glossary and subsection 127.1(2), the Qualifying Income Limit is calculated by the formula:

where A is nil ($0) if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $10,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000. Thus, while Budget 2019 eliminated prior-year taxable income from the 35% expenditure limit calculation, prior-year taxable income still determines whether a CCPC is a Qualifying Corporation entitled to a 40% cash refund on the basic 15% ITC earned on expenditures exceeding its expenditure limit.

Conversely, a Non-Qualifying CCPC (a CCPC other than a qualifying or excluded corporation, whose prior-year taxable income exceeded its Qualifying Income Limit) still receives a 100% refund on the enhanced 35% ITC earned on current expenditures (and PPA) up to its expenditure limit and a 40% refund on the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures up to its expenditure limit under subsection 127.1(2.01), but receives 0% refund (non-refundable) on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding its expenditure limit. Under amended subsection 127.1(2.01), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) (that is not an excluded corporation) receives the exact same refundability profile as a Non-Qualifying CCPC: 100% refund on the 35% ITC for current expenditures and PPA up to its $6 million expenditure limit, 40% refund on the 35% ITC for capital expenditures up to its expenditure limit, and 0% refund (non-refundable) on the 15% basic ITC for expenditures above its expenditure limit. An Excluded Corporation has its refund rate capped at 40% on the 35% ITC for both current and capital expenditures up to the limit, and 40% on the 15% ITC above the limit. Finally, SR&ED ITCs earned on repayments of government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments are never refundable (0% refund rate), though they may be applied against Part I tax payable or carried back 3 years / forward 20 years.

body.text: 3.5 Carryback, Carryforward, Loss Restriction Events, and ITC Recapture Rules
A. Carryover Periods and Ordering Election

Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs (or refundable ITCs that a claimant chooses not to have refunded) may be carried back up to 3 taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years under subsection 127(5) to offset federal Part I income tax otherwise payable. As established in Ainsworth Lumber Co. v. The Queen (2001 TCC), because the statute states that a taxpayer "may" deduct ITCs, the taxpayer has the right to elect the order in which it utilizes refundable versus non-refundable credits. Concurrently, unused balances in the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures carry forward indefinitely (except for partnerships, which must deduct the full pool balance annually under paragraph 96(1)(e.1)).
B. Acquisition of Control / Loss Restriction Events
When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (a "loss restriction event"), strict streaming restrictions are triggered:

items: Section 37 Pool Streaming (Paragraph 37(1)(h) and Subsection 37(6.1)): The corporation's undeducted Section 37 pool balance is reduced to nil at the time control is acquired. Those pre-acquisition SR&ED pool expenditures (including post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures under amended clause 37(6.1)(a)(i)(B)) may only be reinstated and deducted in subsequent taxation years if the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of the corporation's income for that year from that same business or a similar business.

Section 127 ITC Streaming: Similarly, an acquisition of control restricts the carryforward of unused ITCs earned before the acquisition of control and restricts the carryback of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control.

body.text: C. The 20-Year ITC Recapture Regime (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

To ensure that SR&ED tax credits subsidize only the net cost of conducting R&D rather than commercial inventory or commercial production equipment, subsections 127(27) through 127(36) of the ITA impose an ITC Recapture mechanism. All four statutory conditions must be met to trigger recapture in a taxation year:

items: The claimant acquired a particular property in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years under subsections 127(27)(a) and 127(36) to match the 20-year ITC carryforward window);

The cost of the particular property was claimed as a qualified SR&ED expenditure (specifically: materials transformed, post-December 15, 2024 or pre-2014 SR&ED capital property, or first-term / second-term Shared-Use Equipment);
The cost was included in an amount, a percentage of which can reasonably be considered to have been included in computing the claimant's ITC at the end of a taxation year; and
The claimant disposes of or converts to commercial use the particular property (or another property that incorporates the particular property) in the taxation year.

body.text: When triggered, the recaptured amount is added directly to the taxpayer's Part I income tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion (reported in Part 17, Line F3 of Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations or page 5, Line 3 of Form T2038(IND) for individuals). The recapture amount is calculated using the ITC rate at which the credit was earned (15% basic rate, or 20% prior to 2014) applied to the lesser of the cost of the property or its proceeds of disposition (in an arm's length sale) / fair market value (FMV, in a non-arm's length disposition or conversion to commercial use). Correspondingly, any SR&ED ITC recaptured in a taxation year is added back to the claimant's Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures in the immediately following taxation year under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and 37(1)(c.3) (Line 453 of Form T661).
Key statutory exceptions to ITC recapture include:

items: Salaries, Overhead, and Materials Consumed: Salaries, PPA/overhead, and materials consumed do not attract recapture (unless insurance payouts or proceeds received on consumed materials exceed 10% of the cost of the materials).

The 10% De Minimis Scrap Rule: Under the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, no recapture applies if an experimental product or transformed material is sold as scrap for proceeds of disposition (or converted/transferred at an FMV) that are less than 10% of the total cost of the property.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) Conversion Standard: Because SUE is already used partially for commercial purposes during its first and second periods, recapture is triggered on SUE only if the equipment is sold or if its SR&ED usage becomes merely incidental—that is, when all or substantially all (90% or more) of the property has been converted to commercial use.

Non-Arm's Length Transfers (Subsection 127(33)): Recapture does not apply if a claimant disposes of SR&ED capital property to a non-arm's length purchaser in circumstances where the property continues to qualify as ASA (90% or more) capital property for SR&ED.

body.text: 4. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework
4.1 Statutory Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1)

The legal threshold for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED is codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. As Justice Hogan observed in 1726437 Ontario Inc. (o/a AirMax Technologies) v. The Queen (2012 TCC 376), subsection 248(1) operates on a "catch and release" structure:

items: The Preamble: Defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis".
The "Catch" — Core Qualifying Categories (Paragraphs (a), (b), and (c)):
Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

The "Catch" — Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)): Work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada.

The "Release" — Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)): Subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes work with respect to: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; or (k) routine data collection.

body.text: 4.2 Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance: From the Five Questions to the "Why" and "How" Requirements

While the statutory wording of subsection 248(1) has remained unchanged since the 1992 legislative clarifications following the May 1985 Budget Papers, the CRA's administrative framework for evaluating technical eligibility has evolved through four distinct eras:

items: Pre-1985 (Interpretation Bulletin IT-439): Early administrative guidance under IT-439 proved insufficient to clarify eligible "research" and "development" for industrial claimants.

1986–2012 (Information Circular IC 86-4 and IC 86-4R3): Following the May 1985 introduction of the term "experimental development" and a March 4, 1986 policy accord between the Department of Finance and Revenue Canada, the agency released IC 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development, updated as IC 86-4R3 in 1994), which established the three cornerstone criteria: (1) Scientific or technological advancement, (2) Scientific or technological uncertainty, and (3) Scientific and technical content.

2012–2021 (The Five Questions — Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy): In 1998, Judge Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada rendered the landmark decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, linking the three criteria with the statutory definition through a five-question test (subsequently adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada [1998] and CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada [2001 FCA 393]). Published in 2012 and revised on April 24, 2015, the CRA's Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy formalized the Five Questions in Section 2.1:
Question 1 (2.1.1): Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Question 2 (2.1.2): Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Question 3 (2.1.3): Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Question 4 (2.1.4): Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Question 5 (2.1.5): Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

August 2021–Present (The Two Requirements: "Why" and "How" — Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives): On August 13, 2021, the CRA archived the 2015 policy and published the current Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, replacing the five questions with Two Requirements: the "Why" Requirement (derived from paragraphs 248(1)(a)–(c)) and the "How" Requirement (derived from the preamble of subsection 248(1)). Crucially, as the Federal Court of Appeal held in National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2022 FCA 72), the CRA's 2021 reorganization into the "Why" and "How" requirements did not relax the legal standard or supersede Northwest Hydraulic; both frameworks embody the same underlying discipline, and Canadian courts continue to apply the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as binding precedent.

body.text: 4.3 The "Why" Requirement: Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Advancement

Under the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives (and Questions 1 and 4 of Northwest Hydraulic), the "Why" Requirement examines the purpose of the work: it must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement by attempting to resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty.

Scientific or technological uncertainty arises when whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, is not known or cannot be determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience (encompassing both internal business knowledge and publicly available knowledge accessible to competent professionals in the field). As Justice Bowman defined in Northwest Hydraulic, "routine engineering" encompasses techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field; if the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering, there is no technological uncertainty. Importantly, Northwest Hydraulic (and subsequent Tax Court rulings such as Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18, DAZZM Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129, and Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7) established that system uncertainty qualifies as technological uncertainty even when the underlying individual components are known, provided their integration or interaction within a complex system creates unpredictable technological conflicts or interlocking constraints that cannot be resolved by available engineering methods.

The CRA guidelines identify seven diagnostic characteristics indicating that available technological knowledge is insufficient: (1) existing design methods are not applicable; (2) requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; (3) too many variables or unknowns exist; (4) parameters or conditions lie outside the normal operating range; (5) the nature of the problem is evolving; (6) data is not readily available; or (7) interlocking constraints exist. Cost targets alone do not create technological uncertainty, though attempting to achieve cost targets may introduce technical uncertainties.

To satisfy the "Why" requirement, the work must seek to generate or discover conceptual knowledge (such as theories or prediction models) that advances understanding of the underlying science or technology (Line 246 of Form T661), rather than merely collecting factual data or advancing the claimant's business practices. If an uncertainty is circumvented using existing available knowledge or left unaddressed, the work is not eligible. Similarly, acquiring available knowledge or know-how through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve technological advancement (as affirmed in Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42, and Béton Mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 278). Conversely, both the CRA guidelines and Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic (as well as Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, 1999 TCC) establish that failure to achieve the commercial or technical objective does not disqualify a project: the rejection of a hypothesis after testing is nonetheless an advancement because it eliminates a hitherto untested hypothesis and reinforces the measure of technological uncertainty.
4.4 The "How" Requirement: Systematic Investigation, Hypotheses, and Contemporaneous Records

The "How" Requirement (corresponding to Questions 2, 3, and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic) mandates that the work be carried out through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Simply carrying out work in a standard systematic approach (following routine procedures or standards) or engaging in trial-and-error prototyping is not sufficient. Both the CRA guidelines and the Tax Court require four sequential elements:

items: Hypothesis / Idea Generation: Following the observation of the subject matter of the problem, formulation of a clear objective, and identification of the technological uncertainty, the claimant must generate an idea consistent with known facts to serve as a starting point for further investigation towards resolving the problem (expressed as a possible solution, proposed method, or approach—referred to as a hypothesis).

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: The claimant must methodically test the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment (such as building and testing a prototype in an industrial context) or analysis, allowing the idea or hypothesis to evolve and be modified as a result of testing.
Developing Logical Conclusions: The claimant must develop logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis.

Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Evidence of the hypotheses tested and results obtained must be generated and kept as the work progresses. While the Tax Court has occasionally accepted highly credible oral evidence where written documentation was sparse (e.g., Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313), the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) and the Tax Court in Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 183) and Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63) have consistently dismissed claims where records were reconstructed after the fact, vague, or conclusory.

body.text: 4.5 Eligible Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)) Versus Excluded Work (Paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k))

Once a claimant establishes that core SR&ED work exists under paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b), or (c), the scope of eligible work expands under paragraph 248(1)(d) to include support work that falls within one of the eight statutory categories—(1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research—provided that it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada.

Support work is never SR&ED on its own. Because activities such as "testing" and "data collection" appear in both paragraph 248(1)(d) (as eligible support work) and paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k) (as excluded "routine testing" and "routine data collection"), the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives establish that the key feature distinguishing eligible support work from excluded work is purpose (Why was the work done?). If data collection or testing is carried out specifically to perform or directly support the SR&ED work, it is eligible as support work. Conversely, if activities are performed as routine actions to support standard business operations (such as routine data collection for quality control or quality assurance), they are excluded—even if the data collected later turns out to be useful for SR&ED work. (Note: For taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026, regulatory and certification testing directly related to an eligible SR&ED project for initial commercialization approval becomes eligible under the Budget 2026 expansion).
5. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures and Calculation Methodologies
5.1 Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged vs. Directly Attributable Labour

Salaries and wages represent the core expenditure component of Canadian SR&ED claims and are governed by subsection 37(8), subsection 78(4), and subsection 248(1) of the ITA, subsections 2900(2) and 2900(4)–(10) of the ITR, and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025). Only income from an office or employment (such as gross wages reported on a T4 slip or permissible foreign salary) qualifies as "salary or wages"; distributions of income to partners, dividends, retiring allowances, stock option benefits, extended vacation or sick leave, and the employer's share of related payroll benefits are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages.

The classification of employee labour depends on whether the employee is directly engaged in SR&ED or performs directly attributable support/administrative functions, and whether the claimant elects the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method.

Employees Directly Engaged in SR&ED (Lines 300, 305, 307, and 309 of Form T661) are eligible under both the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method. "Directly engaged" refers strictly to hands-on work determined by the actual tasks performed rather than the job title of the employee. Qualifying tasks for directly engaged employees include: (1) experimentation and analysis; (2) support work in engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research; (3) tasks performed by non-specialized employees (such as operating a machine for an experiment that requires the use of that machine, or feeding raw materials into a machine, provided the non-specialized employee's work is supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications); (4) direct supervision of employees performing SR&ED and SR&ED contract administration (technical input only, excluding work beyond first-line supervision); and (5) technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects (such as assignment of technological personnel, job priorities, development of technological strategies, and quality of materials used), technological feasibility studies relating to SR&ED projects, and technical documentation for internal use. Under subsection 37(8), if an employee spends all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of their time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is deemed to be for SR&ED; otherwise, only the portion reasonably considered to relate to the time spent performing SR&ED may be claimed.

Employees Not Directly Engaged — Directly Attributable Administrative/Support Labour (Line 360 of Form T661) cannot be claimed on Lines 300–309 and are excluded from specific tracking under the Proxy Method (as they are covered by the 55% PPA). Under the Traditional Method, salary or wages for clerical and administrative staff (such as accounting, payroll, finance, legal support, purchasing, human resources, or shipping) or other employees who support the performance of SR&ED without being directly engaged may be claimed as overhead on Line 360 only if the functions are non-technological, aid ongoing SR&ED, and pass both the "directly related" and "incremental" tests (for example, time spent by a personnel manager specifically hiring dedicated SR&ED staff meets the directly related test, whereas executive managerial oversight does not).
5.2 Specified Employees: Ownership Thresholds, Bonus Exclusions, and YMPE Caps (2023–2027)

To prevent significant shareholders and non-arm's length employees from channelling corporate profits into inflated SR&ED salary and proxy claims, the ITA and ITR impose strict statutory caps on Specified Employees. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a specified employee of a taxpayer is an employee who is a specified shareholder owning 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation (or a related corporation), or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer.
Specified employees are subject to three mandatory statutory restrictions:

items: Complete Exclusion of Bonuses and Remuneration Based on Profits: For non-specified employees, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are eligible for the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (though excluded from the PPA salary base). For a specified employee, bonuses and remuneration based on profits are 100% excluded from both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Lines 305/309) and the PPA salary base.

Pool of Deductible Expenditures Cap (5 × YMPE): The maximum amount of directly engaged SR&ED salary or wages (including taxable benefits and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year, but excluding bonuses and profit-based remuneration) that may be included in the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap (Lesser of 75% of Salary or 2.5 × YMPE — ITR Subsection 2900(7)): When calculating the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 for the 55% PPA, the includable salary for each specified employee is restricted to the lesser of:

75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid salary or wages paid in the year); and

2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for the time during the year that the employee was not a specified employee): PPA Salary Base Cap = 2.5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual ÷ 365)

body.text: 5.3 Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada

As a general rule under subsections 37(1), 37(2), and 127(9) of the ITA, SR&ED work performed physically outside Canada (and outside Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone under subsection 37(1.3)) cannot be included in the Section 37 pool or earn an SR&ED ITC. The sole statutory exception is codified in subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA (reported on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661), which allows a claimant to claim "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work performed outside Canada if all five of the following cumulative criteria are met:

items: The SR&ED work outside Canada was performed directly by an employee of the claimant and not a contractor;
The employee who performed the work was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred;
The work was related to the business of the claimant;
The work done outside Canada was an integral part of, and solely in support of, the SR&ED project carried out in Canada; and
The salary or wages paid are not subject to income or profits tax from another country.

body.text: Under subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA, the permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada are subject to a statutory limit (10% of the directly engaged SR&ED salary and wages incurred for work performed in Canada).
5.4 Unpaid Remuneration and Current Expenditures: The 180-Day Rule
Two separate statutory provisions govern accrued SR&ED expenses that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which they were incurred:

items: Unpaid Salaries and Wages (Subsection 78(4) of the ITA — Lines 310 and 315 of Form T661): Under subsection 78(4), any salary, wages, or other remuneration incurred in a taxation year that is not paid within 180 days of the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year for both Section 37 pool deduction purposes and Section 127 ITC purposes. The claimant must report the unpaid salary on Line 315 of Form T661 (and must not include it on Lines 300–309 or Line 360). When the salary is subsequently paid in a later taxation year, it is deemed incurred in that payment year and is claimed on Line 310 of Form T661 for that subsequent year (though prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year on Line 310 remain excluded from the PPA salary base under ITR subsection 2900(9)).

Unpaid Current Expenditures Other Than Salaries/Wages (Subsection 127(26) of the ITA — Lines 500 and 520 of Form T661): For non-salary current expenditures (such as materials, arm's length contracts, third-party payments, lease costs, or overhead), an amount unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year is still included in the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures in the year incurred, but under subsection 127(26) it is deemed not to have been incurred in that year for Section 127 ITC purposes. The unpaid expenditure must be subtracted in Part 4 on Line 520 of Form T661. In the subsequent taxation year when the liability is actually paid, the claimant adds the paid amount back to qualified expenditures on Line 500 (note: if the unpaid item was an arm's length SR&ED contract or third-party payment, only 80% of the subsequent payment is added on Line 500).

body.text: 5.5 Overhead Calculation Methods: Prescribed Proxy Amount (55% PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Every SR&ED claimant must choose between two mutually exclusive statutory methods for claiming SR&ED overhead and other indirect expenditures on Form T661: the Proxy Method (elected by ticking Line 160 under subsection 37(10) of the ITA) or the Traditional Method (chosen by ticking Line 162, or applied by default if no election is made). Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is statutorily irrevocable for that taxation year.
A. The Proxy Method and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method on Line 160, it does not track, allocate, or deduct specific SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the claimant computes a notional substitute amount in Part 5 of Form T661—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the salary base under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR, subject to the Overall PPA Cap:
PPA = 55% × Salary Base (not exceeding the Overall PPA Cap)

The Salary Base (Part 5, Section A of Form T661) comprises the directly engaged SR&ED salaries and wages of employees (Lines 300, 305, 307, and 309), subject to five universal exclusions for ALL employees under ITR subsection 2900(9)—(1) taxable benefits, (2) prior-year unpaid salaries paid in the year (Line 310), (3) remuneration based on profits, (4) bonuses, and (5) the employer's share of related benefits—plus the specified employee caps (lesser of 75% of total eligible salary or 2.5 × YMPE) under ITR subsection 2900(7). Because the PPA is a notional calculation, it is never included in the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures; instead, the claimant deducts its actual business overhead expenses as ordinary business expenses, while the notional PPA is added on Line 502 of Form T661 to earn the Section 127 SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (at 35% or 15%).

To ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and other specific deductions do not exceed total business expenditures made in the taxation year, ITR subsection 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA calculated by the formula:
Overall PPA Cap = A − (B + C)

where A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the total of specific deductions claimed under section 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, and bad debts), section 24, section 26, section 30, section 32, section 37 (SR&ED pool deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), sections 66 to 66.8, and section 104 of the ITA; and C is the total expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as building rent).
B. The Traditional Method

When a claimant selects the Traditional Method on Line 162, it enters "0" on Line 502 (no PPA is calculated) and instead specifically identifies, tracks, allocates, and claims its actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the ITR, overhead and other expenditures claimed on Line 360 are included in both the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and the Section 127 Qualified Expenditures for ITC purposes, provided the claimant proves that each expenditure satisfies two cumulative legal tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: There must be a direct linkage—with no intervening step or intermediary—between the expenditure and either (i) the SR&ED work, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure (or the claimed portion thereof) would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada not occurred.
