body.text: 5.6 Treatment of Cloud Computing, Software Licences, and Utilities

A frequent area of audit adjustment in Canadian technology, engineering, and design studio claims involves the treatment of cloud computing infrastructure (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud), computer-aided design (CAD) subscriptions, software-as-a-service (SaaS) licences, and telecommunications/utilities:

items: Cloud Computing and SaaS Software Subscriptions Under the Proxy Method: As practitioner analyses emphasize, the statutory categories of current SR&ED expenditures under the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA) are closed and exhaustive: they consist solely of directly engaged salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, SR&ED contracts performed on the claimant's behalf, third-party payments, and post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs. A cloud simulation subscription or a CAD/SaaS software licence does not constitute "materials consumed or transformed" (which must be physical and tangible—solid, liquid, or gas—under the Materials for SR&ED Policy) and is covered by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4); claiming a cloud or software subscription separately under the Proxy Method is disallowed as claiming overhead twice.

Purchased Software, Hardware, and Cloud Costs Under the Traditional Method and Capital Rules: Following the post-December 15, 2024 restoration of capital expenditures under Bill C-15 (and parallel provincial updates such as Ontario's 2026 Fall Economic Statement), computers, high-performance computing equipment, software and hardware testing tools, prototyping equipment, and software bought outright as depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures (if intended to be used 90% or more [ASA] for SR&ED) or as Shared-Use Equipment (if new and used >50% for SR&ED). Under the Traditional Method, incremental development costs must be strictly separated from commercial production hosting and fixed monthly telephone, cellular, or internet fees (which the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy explicitly disallows as fixed ordinary business expenses that would be incurred regardless of SR&ED, whereas specific identifiable charges such as incremental long-distance charges may qualify).

body.text: 5.7 Materials Consumed Versus Materials Transformed and the "Body of a Thing" Test

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) (Traditional Method), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR, and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, a claimant may claim the cost of materials consumed (Line 320 of Form T661) or materials transformed (Line 325 of Form T661) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

To qualify as "materials for SR&ED" (as opposed to general laboratory supplies or overhead), an item must pass the strict "Body of a Thing" Test established in Sections 4.0 to 4.2 of the Materials for SR&ED Policy:

items: Physical and Tangible: The raw materials, substances, or items must be physical and tangible—existing in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state.

Composing the Body of a Tangible Object: At a given moment in the SR&ED process, the items must compose the body of either (i) a tangible object ("thing") on which the SR&ED is being carried out, or (ii) a tangible object (an intermediate product, by-product, or final product) that results from the SR&ED being carried out.

body.text: Consequently, laboratory glassware and supplies (test tubes, pipettes, petri dishes, vials, bottles, beakers, flasks, dishes, filter papers), broken or used lab supplies, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants such as engine oil, and general utilities (electricity, natural gas, water, oil, propane) do not meet the interpretation of "materials for SR&ED" and cannot be claimed on Lines 320 or 325 (though their cost or a portion thereof may qualify as SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 under the Traditional Method).
For items that pass the "body of a thing" test, the distinction between Line 320 and Line 325 governs future ITC recapture exposure:

items: Materials Consumed (Line 320): Materials that are used up, destroyed, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED testing process (having no residual value or use after testing). Examples include seed, growth media, agar, fungal culture ingredients, fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides used in test plots, cardboard boxes and ink destroyed in printing tests, or galvanized metal parts tested to destruction. Materials consumed do not trigger ITC recapture (unless proceeds such as insurance payouts exceed 10% of the cost of the materials).

Materials Transformed (Line 325): Materials that have been changed, converted, or incorporated into another physical material or product during the SR&ED process where the material still retains some value either to the claimant or to another party (including recycled SR&ED materials). If transformed materials (or the product incorporating them) are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, ITC recapture rules apply under subsections 127(27) to 127(36).

Timing and Valuation: The cost of materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (not when received from a supplier, removed from inventory, or manufactured without experimental development), and must be paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year to earn an ITC in that year. Costs include invoice costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, storage costs, and other acquisition costs, but purchases from non-arm's length suppliers are limited to the cost incurred by the non-arm's length party (excluding any profit element) for ITC purposes under subsection 127(11.6) (Line 542).

body.text: 5.8 Subcontractor Expenditures (Arm's Length 80% Rule vs. Non-Arm's Length Transfers) and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant engages external entities to perform SR&ED work in Canada, the tax treatment depends on whether the relationship is an arm's length contract, a non-arm's length (NAL) contract, or a third-party payment:

items: Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340 of Form T661): Where a claimant (payer) contracts an arm's length contractor to perform SR&ED in Canada on behalf of the claimant (meaning the work is controlled by the payer, rights to the work are exclusive to the payer, the contract is generally limited to one payer, has a commercial focus, and is accounted for on an accrual basis):
Section 37 Pool: 100% of the contract expenditure is included in the payer's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures.
Section 127 ITC Base (The 80% Rule): Only 80% of the arm's length contract expenditure qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (20% is subtracted on Line 529 of Form T661).

Taxable Supplier Requirement: To qualify for the ITC, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier"; an SR&ED contract expenditure paid or payable to a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier is excluded from qualified expenditures.

Elimination of Capital Look-Through Reduction Post-December 15, 2024: Following the Bill C-15 restoration of capital expenditures, contract expenditures and third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024 are generally no longer reduced by the amount of any related expenditure of the SR&ED performer that is of a capital nature (for depreciable property or equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024).
Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Line 345 of Form T661 and Form T1146): Where a claimant contracts a non-arm's length person or partnership to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada:

Payer Treatment: The payer includes 100% of the NAL contract expenditure in its Section 37 deductible pool (Line 345), but under paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), 0% of the NAL contract expenditure qualifies for an ITC directly in the hands of the payer (100% is subtracted on Line 541 of Form T661).

Performer Treatment and Form T1146 Transfer: Simultaneously, the amount received or receivable by the NAL performer is not considered to be a contract payment under subsection 127(9), so it does not reduce the NAL performer's own qualified SR&ED expenditures. The NAL performer may claim its own SR&ED expenditures and ITCs, or the payer and the NAL performer may jointly complete and sign Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsections 127(13) to 127(15) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures to the payer (reported on Line 508 of the payer's T661 and deducted on Line 544 of the performer's T661, capped at the amount the performer's qualified expenditures would otherwise be at year-end).

Third-Party Payments (Line 370 of Form T661 and Form T1263): A third-party payment is a payment made to an approved association, university, college, research institute, granting organization, or other approved entity (or in certain cases a Canadian resident corporation or tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation) for SR&ED carried out in Canada that is controlled by the performer, where rights to the work are non-exclusive (generally published) with a preferential right to the payer to exploit the results, there is usually more than one payer, the work is often basic or applied research related to the claimant's business, and tax treatment is on a cash basis. Third-party payments are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 80% eligible for the SR&ED ITC (20% subtracted on Line 529). Claimants do not submit Part 2 project information on Form T661 for third-party payments, but must complete and attach Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) for each payment.

body.text: 5.9 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

One of the most significant operational changes enacted by Bill C-15 (following the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025) is the full restoration of capital and lease expenditure incentives for property acquired (and available for use under subsection 13(27) and subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024). Property acquired before December 16, 2024 (after December 31, 2013) remains strictly ineligible. The restored regime operates across three distinct tracks.
A. SR&ED Capital Expenditures — The 90% "All or Substantially All" (ASA) Track (Line 390 of Form T661)

Under restored paragraph 37(1)(b), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) (Traditional Method) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) (Proxy Method) of the ITA, and amended paragraph 2902(b) of the ITR, an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that either:

items: The property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada; or
All or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its value would be consumed in the performance of SR&ED in Canada.

body.text: Key legal rules governing ASA capital expenditures include:

items: 100% Deduction and ITC Eligibility: If the property is brand new when acquired, 100% of its capital cost is included in the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (providing an immediate 100% write-off against income, deemed to be CCA under subsection 37(6), so the asset must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8) and 100% of its capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (at the 35% enhanced rate—40% refundable—or the 15% basic rate).

New vs. Used Equipment Distinction: If the depreciable property is used equipment (previously acquired for use, lease, or any purpose by a prior owner, such as demonstration equipment), its cost can still be included on Line 390 in the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures for an income tax deduction, but it is a prescribed expenditure under paragraph 2902(b) of the ITR and must be subtracted on Line 530 / Line 535 of Form T661, earning 0% ITC. However, under the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), if used equipment is refurbished by a vendor prior to acquisition and those refurbishments are so significant that the equipment can be said to be in a "new state" (producing the same useful life as newly manufactured equipment), the expenditure qualifies for the ITC; if the claimant carries out significant refurbishments after acquiring used equipment, the costs of the refurbishments may qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure.

Exclusion of Land and Buildings: Non-depreciable assets (such as land or goodwill), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are strictly excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e).

Form T661 Reporting: Claimants must report the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024 and their percentage of SR&ED operating time on Lines 262 and 263 of Part 2 of Form T661.

body.text: B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) — The >50% "Primarily Used" Track (Line 504 of Form T661)

Where a claimant acquires new depreciable equipment after December 15, 2024 that is used for both SR&ED and commercial work—failing the 90% ASA intended-use test—it may qualify as First Term and Second Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) of the ITA and the SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026). To qualify as SUE, the property must:

items: Be brand new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024;
Not be general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF);

Not be a Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the ITR—defined as a building, or equipment intended at the time of acquisition to be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a facility, plant, or line for commercial manufacturing, commercial processing, or other commercial purpose, and intended over its expected useful life to be used primarily (>50%) for purposes other than SR&ED; and
Actually be used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its actual operating time) for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada during the applicable statutory period:

First Term SUE: Tested over the First Period, which starts when the equipment is acquired (available for use) and ends at the end of the first taxation year that occurs at least 12 months after that acquisition time. If actual SR&ED operating time exceeds 50% during the First Period, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost of the equipment qualifies for the SR&ED ITC on Line 504 in that taxation year.

Second Term SUE: Tested over the Second Period, which starts when the equipment is acquired (available for use) and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that acquisition time. Provided the equipment qualified as First Term SUE and actual SR&ED operating time exceeds 50% over the Second Period, an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC on Line 504 in that second taxation year—bringing total qualified expenditures to 50% of the equipment's capital cost across the two periods.

body.text: Unlike 90% ASA capital property, the capital cost of SUE is not part of the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures; instead, the claimant depreciates SUE under the regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rates and rules on Schedule T2SCH8 (and any ITC earned on SUE and applied or refunded reduces the undepreciated capital cost [UCC] of the CCA class in the subsequent year). Claimants must name the 20 most expensive SUE properties acquired after December 15, 2024 on Form T661.
C. Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada qualify under rules that depend on the claimant's overhead election:

items: Under the Traditional Method: When leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% of the expenditure can be claimed as a lease cost (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)); when used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, the lease cost is claimed on Line 360 as an overhead expenditure proportional to the percentage of operating time used for SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II)). Under the Traditional Method, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for leased land may also qualify under overhead and other expenditures if ASA or directly attributable to SR&ED.

Under the Proxy Method: Lease costs for general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) and lease costs for land cannot be claimed. For non-GPOEF leased equipment, if used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); if used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED, 50% of the lease cost is claimable (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); and if used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED, 0% is claimable.

Building Rent Exclusion: Outlays and expenses for the use of, or right to use, a building (rent) are specifically excluded under both methods (subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii) and paragraph 37(8)(e)), with the sole exception of lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance under section 2903 of the ITR.

body.text: 6. Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Grant Stacking Mechanics
6.1 Statutory Definitions of Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA, both the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and the Section 127 Qualified SR&ED Expenditures must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the income tax return filing due date for the taxation year (Lines 429–432 and Lines 513–517 of Form T661).

items: Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9)): Defined as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. This includes direct federal grants (such as NRC IRAP contributions), provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario OITC/ORDTC/OBRITC, Québec CRIC, Alberta IEG, and BC SR&ED credit), indirect assistance from government-funded non-profits, funding from Crown corporations or foreign governments, and forgivable or conditionally repayable loans (where repayment is conditional on earning profits/revenues or characterized as royalties, as affirmed in CAE Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA). However, effective January 1, 2020 (for loans made after December 31, 2019), "government assistance" does not include an "excluded loan" as defined in subsection 12(11) of the ITA.

Non-Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9) and Paragraph 12(1)(x)): Defined as any amount that would be included in a claimant's income under paragraph 12(1)(x) of the ITA (read without reference to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii))—namely, an amount received as an inducement, reimbursement, contribution, allowance, grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, or other assistance from a non-government entity for the cost of a property or for an outlay or expense.

Contract Payments (Subsection 127(9)): An amount paid or payable to a claimant by an arm's length taxable supplier for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of a person or partnership entitled to a deduction as a current expenditure or third-party payment, or an amount for a current expenditure payable by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or Part I tax-exempt entity for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf.

Asymmetric Impact on Pool vs. ITC: A contract payment reduces the performer's Section 127 Qualified Expenditures for ITC purposes (to avoid duplication of the ITC), but it does NOT reduce the performer's Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures.

Deliverable Goods vs. Contract for SR&ED (Com Dev Ltd. Precedent): As established in Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (1999 TCC), if a customer contracts under a fixed-price contract where the taxpayer bears the risk rather than purchasing SR&ED services on the payer's behalf, the payment is commercial revenue—not a "contract payment"—and the performer retains its SR&ED ITCs.

body.text: 6.2 Timing of Reductions, Assistance Allocations, and Repayments

items: Accrual Cutoff at the Filing Due Date: Assistance or contract payments reduce SR&ED pools for a taxation year if, on or before the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date (6 months after year-end for corporations and deemed partnerships under subsection 127(23)), the amount has been received, is entitled to be received, or can reasonably be expected to be received. Because current-year provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario OITC, Québec CRIC, and BC SR&ED credit) are reasonably expected to be received by the filing due date, the current year's provincial R&D tax credit reduces the current year's federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool in the same taxation year.

Exception for Provincial Credits Attributable to the Notional PPA: Under Section 4.5.3 of the Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and the Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is not included in the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit (such as the Ontario OITC or legacy Québec R&D credit) related to the PPA (or salaries not included in the Section 37 pool) reduces qualified expenditures for ITC purposes, but is not assistance for the purposes of calculating the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, that portion is added directly to income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year it is received.

Project-by-Project Reduction and Excess Assistance Allocation (Form T1145): Under subsections 127(18) to 127(22), assistance reduces qualified expenditures on a project-by-project basis and cannot reduce a project's expenditures below nil (any excess is included in income, or, if the project is performed by a non-arm's length group, must be allocated to other group members using Form T1145, Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, reported on Line 538 of Form T661).

Repayments of Assistance (Paragraph 37(1)(c) and Subsections 127(10.7)–(10.8)): When a claimant repays government or non-government assistance or a contract payment that previously reduced its SR&ED claim, the repayment increases the Section 37 pool on Line 445 and is added to the ITC calculation on Line 560 of Form T661 (Schedule T2SCH31, Line 370). The repayment earns an ITC at the rate (15% or 35%) in effect in the year the assistance was originally applied, but because repayments are not qualified expenditures, that ITC is non-refundable in the year of repayment (though it can reduce taxes payable, or be carried back 3 years / forward 20 years).

body.text: 6.3 Coordinating SR&ED with NRC IRAP, Strategic Innovation/Response Funds, and Clean Technology ITCs

Canadian businesses routinely "stack" direct federal and provincial innovation grants with federal and provincial SR&ED tax credits. While receiving a direct government grant does not prevent work from being eligible for SR&ED, only the net expenditure (after deducting the grant as government assistance) earns the SR&ED ITC, and program rules cited in industry grant guides generally cap total combined government assistance from all sources at 75% of total eligible project costs (up to 90% for specific clean technology, Indigenous, or rural project types):

items: National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP): Managed by the National Research Council Canada through Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs), NRC IRAP provides non-repayable cost-shared financial contributions to incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer full-time employees (sole proprietorships and partnerships are ineligible for IRAP). According to grant advisory benchmarks, standard IRAP awards have a median of approximately $75,000 (with typical ranges of $50,000 to $1,000,000, NRC published service standards covering decisions from under $50,000 up to $10 million, and specialized streams such as the IRAP Clean Technology Program and the $244.2 million Defence Industry Assist stream announced in January 2026). IRAP covers up to 80% of eligible internal R&D labour costs and up to 50% of eligible subcontractor costs for projects at Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) 3 to 7 that are approved before work begins.

Critical IRAP + SR&ED Proxy Stacking Mechanic: When a CCPC receives an IRAP grant covering 80% of its directly engaged R&D salaries, the IRAP grant reduces the net qualified expenditure pool on Lines 431 and 515 of Form T661. However, under ITR subsection 2900(4) and CRA administrative guidance (as illustrated in the CRA's Guidance: How the Canada Emergency Wage Subsidy Affects SR&ED Claims), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated on 100% of the gross eligible SR&ED salary base BEFORE deducting the wage assistance. Consequently, the claimant earns the 35% SR&ED ITC not only on the 20% unfunded portion of its R&D salaries, but also on the entire 55% overhead proxy generated by 100% of the R&D salaries.

Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) / Strategic Response Fund ($5 Billion): Managed by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) for large-scale industrial R&D and scale-up projects (typically carrying an implicit $10 million-plus project floor, transitioning into the $5 billion Strategic Response Fund alongside the $25 billion Canada Strong Fund announced on April 27, 2026). Both non-repayable contributions and repayable contributions from SIF or Regional Development Agencies (such as FedDev Ontario, PrairiesCan, PacifiCan, and ACOA) constitute government assistance that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures upon entitlement/receipt, and later generates non-refundable SR&ED ITCs on Line 560 as repayments are made.

Clean Technology Investment Tax Credit (30% Refundable ITC): Provides a 30% refundable tax credit on eligible clean-technology capital property through 2033 (and 15% in 2034). Because a taxpayer cannot claim two federal credits on the exact same dollar of expense, optimal structuring routes R&D labour, materials, and test rigs to IRAP and SR&ED (35% refundable) and commercial clean-technology equipment purchases to the 30% Clean Technology ITC.

body.text: 6.4 Comprehensive Financial Modelling: Stacking Federal Grants, Provincial Credits, and Federal SR&ED

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics of stacking NRC IRAP, a provincial R&D tax credit (Ontario's 8% OITC), and the federal 35% SR&ED ITC under the Proxy Method, consider a Qualifying CCPC in Ontario during its 2026 taxation year that incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged non-specified employee SR&ED salaries and $100,000 in consumed materials ($1,100,000 total cash outlay), and receives a $400,000 NRC IRAP grant:

items: Gross Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Line 400 of Form T661): Salaries (Line 300: $1,000,000) + Materials Consumed (Line 320: $100,000) = $1,100,000.
Prescribed Proxy Amount (Part 5 & Line 502 of Form T661): Calculated on 100% of the gross SR&ED salary base ($1,000,000) prior to deducting the IRAP grant: 55% × $1,000,000 = $550,000.
Gross Qualified Expenditures Before Assistance (Line 511 of Form T661): Line 400 ($1,100,000) + Line 502 ($550,000) = $1,650,000.

Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (8% OITC — Schedule 566): Ontario qualified expenditures equal federal gross qualified expenditures ($1,650,000) minus the $400,000 federal IRAP assistance = $1,250,000, yielding a refundable OITC at 8% of $100,000.

Net Federal Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 559 / Line 570 of Form T661): Gross federal qualified expenditures ($1,650,000) are reduced by both the $400,000 NRC IRAP grant (Line 515) and the $100,000 Ontario OITC (Line 513), leaving $1,150,000. (Note: If the CCPC also claims the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit [ORDTC] on Schedule 508, the ORDTC is 3.5% × [$1,250,000 − $100,000] = $40,250, which would further reduce Net Federal Qualified Expenditures to $1,109,750).
Federal SR&ED Refundable ITC (35% — Schedule T2SCH31): 35% × $1,150,000 = $402,500.

Total Combined Cash Recovery: $400,000 (IRAP) + $100,000 (OITC) + $402,500 (Federal SR&ED) = $902,500. On a $1,100,000 actual cash R&D outlay, the corporation recovers $902,500 in non-dilutive cash (82.05% of actual cash expenditure), reducing its net out-of-pocket R&D cost to $197,500.

body.text: 7. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits. Only three Canadian jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut—do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. All provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the federal ITA and therefore reduce the federal Section 37 deductible pool and Section 127 qualified expenditure base.
7.1 Québec: The New Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) and Legacy Regime Transition

In its 2025–2026 Budget (presented on March 25, 2025), the Government of Québec enacted a foundational overhaul of its provincial R&D tax incentive system, replacing eight separate legacy R&D tax measures with a single, standardized, fully refundable incentive: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), administered by Revenu Québec.
A. Transition Timeline: Legacy Credits vs. CRIC

items: Taxation Years Beginning Before March 26, 2025: Claimants continue to file under the legacy Québec R&D tax credit regime (detailed in Guide IN-109-V and Deduction Form RD-222-V), which included the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), and the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, where cumulative fee balances at the end of a taxation year ending after March 25, 2025 remain eligible for a taxation year ending no later than December 31, 2029).

Taxation Years Beginning After March 25, 2025: The legacy R&D tax credits are replaced by the CRIC, which can be claimed by eligible corporations (and corporations that are members of an eligible partnership) that operate a business in Québec, maintain an establishment in Québec, and undertake (or cause to be undertaken on their behalf under a contract) eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec. To claim the CRIC, an eligible corporation completes Form RD-1029.8.CR-T and attaches it to its corporate income tax return.

body.text: B. Expanded Scope of Activities Under the CRIC: R&D Plus Pre-Commercialization
Unlike the legacy Québec credits, the CRIC supports both R&D and pre-commercialization activities in Québec:

items: Scientific Research and Experimental Development (R&D) Activities: Harmonized with federal legislation regarding basic research, applied research, and experimental development (with the CRA continuing to conduct scientific reviews of R&D work).

Eligible Pre-Commercialization Activities: Pre-commercialization activities are eligible if undertaken in conjunction with (as a continuation of) R&D work carried out in Québec by the corporation or on its behalf. Eligible pre-commercialization activities include:

Regulatory Testing and Validation: Tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements and aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification for the purpose of commercializing an innovation;

Product Design: Product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials (as well as prototype development, evaluation of operational constraints, validation by pilot users, and development of usage scenarios/use cases where carried out directly as a continuation of R&D); and
Initial Certification Quality Control: Quality control activities, provided they pertain directly to implementing a quality control system required to obtain an initial approval or certification.

body.text: C. Qualified Expenditures, Exclusion Threshold, and 30% / 20% Refundable Credit Rates
Under the CRIC, qualified expenditures incurred in Québec (net of government and non-government financial assistance) comprise four categories:

items: 100% of salaries or wages paid to the corporation's employees for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec;
50% of the amount paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec;
50% of the payments made to an eligible public research centre, an eligible research consortium, or an eligible university entity; and

Property or equipment acquisition costs used for eligible activities in Québec (excluding costs relating to the acquisition of a building, land, or a right to use a building or land, and excluding property used as part of a large investment project tax holiday). (Note: The portion of the CRIC attributable to property acquisition is recovered by a special tax if, during the minimum period of 730 consecutive days following the beginning of its use, the property ceases to be used solely in Québec for eligible activities, and property claimed under the CRIC cannot be double-claimed under the Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation [C3i]).

body.text: To qualify for the CRIC, a corporation's qualified expenditures in a taxation year must exceed an Applicable Exclusion Threshold, which corresponds to the greater of:

items: $50,000; or

The sum of the basic personal amount (BPA) of the applicable personal income tax system for each employee ($18,952 per employee for 2026, increasing annually), adjusted to reflect the actual time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

body.text: Crucially, the CRIC rate is not based on corporate asset size: every eligible corporation in Québec earns a 100% refundable tax credit at the following two-tier rate structure:

items: 30% refundable rate on the portion of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, up to a maximum of $1,000,000; and
20% refundable rate on qualified expenditures over the $1,000,000 maximum, if applicable.

body.text: For example, if a Québec corporation has $1,500,000 in gross qualified expenditures and an adjusted employee exclusion threshold of $355,350, its net qualified expenditures exceeding the threshold are $1,144,650; it earns 30% on the first $1,000,000 ($300,000) plus 20% on the remaining $144,650 ($28,930), for a total refundable CRIC of $328,930 (or if 25 employees spend 100% of their time on eligible work in 2026, the exclusion threshold is 25 × $18,952 = $473,800, leaving $1,026,200 above the threshold and generating $1,000,000 × 30% + $26,200 × 20% = $305,240).
7.2 Ontario: OITC (8%), ORDTC (3.5%), and OBRITC (20%)

Ontario provides three separate corporate R&D tax credits under the Ontario Taxation Act, 2007 (sections 38–41, 96, and 97), all administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through the federal corporate income tax system. (Practitioners must not confuse Ontario's R&D credits with the acronym "OSRTC", which refers to the Ontario Sound Recording Tax Credit under s. 43.12—a cultural media tax credit administered by Ontario Creates, not an R&D incentive).

Following the Royal Assent of federal Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, and as confirmed in the 2026 Ontario Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review (Fall Economic Statement) and updated Ontario Ministry of Finance guidance (October 30, 2026), Ontario automatically restored the eligibility of 100% of qualified capital expenditures (including software and hardware testing tools, high-performance computing equipment, prototyping equipment, and certain property or lease costs) for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 across both the OITC and the ORDTC:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96; Claimed on Schedule 566):

Rate and Refundability: 8% refundable tax credit (for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016; 10% prior to June 1, 2016) on qualified SR&ED expenditures performed in Ontario up to a $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit, yielding a maximum refundable tax credit of $240,000 per year (shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years).

Eligible Expenditures: Includes 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (40% of pre-2014 capital expenditures; 0% of capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 and before December 16, 2024) attributable to a permanent establishment in Ontario.

Dual Phase-Out Thresholds (Income and Capital): Unlike the federal SR&ED expenditure limit, the Ontario OITC $3 million expenditure limit retains its independent provincial phase-out rules: it is gradually reduced if the corporation's (and associated group's) prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 and is totally eliminated at $800,000, OR if the prior year's taxable capital exceeds $25,000,000 and is totally eliminated at $50,000,000.
Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Claimed on Schedule 508):

Rate and Refundability: 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016; 4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) available to all corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario to reduce Ontario corporate income tax payable. There is no expenditure cap.

Eligible Expenditures and OITC Offset: Includes 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (and 100% of pre-2014 capital expenditures) in Ontario. Because the 8% OITC is a form of government assistance, any OITC claimed reduces the eligible expenditures for the 3.5% ORDTC (whereas the ORDTC itself and the federal SR&ED ITC do not reduce ORDTC eligible expenditures).

Carryovers and Recapture: Unused ORDTC can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years. Recapture rules apply if property included in a previous claim is subsequently disposed of or converted to commercial use, using the 23.56% rate to calculate the recapture amount.
Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97; Claimed on Schedules 568 and 569):

Rate, Cap, and Refundability: 20% refundable tax credit on qualified current expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI)—including Ontario universities or community colleges, hospital research institutes (large teaching hospitals), Ontario Centres of Excellence or federal Networks of Centres of Excellence operating in Ontario, and designated non-profit organizations.

Limits and Conditions: Qualified expenditures are capped at $20,000,000 annually, providing a maximum annual refundable credit of $4,000,000. The corporation must not be "connected" to the ERI (the ERI cannot own shares carrying >10% of voting rights or >10% of the fair market value of all issued shares, or deal at non-arm's length), payments must be made in money (not a payment-in-kind), and small businesses may claim both the 20% OBRITC and the 8% OITC on qualified expenditures.

body.text: 7.3 British Columbia: Permanent 10% SR&ED Tax Credit and Bill 2 (2026) Harmonization

Governed by Part 6 of the British Columbia Income Tax Act and administered by the CRA via Form T666 (British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit) and Schedule 5 (Line 674 for refundable credits; Line 659 for non-refundable credits), British Columbia enacted major enhancements in BC Budget 2026 through Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026:

items: Elimination of Sunset Date (Permanent Enactment): BC Budget 2026 made the BC SR&ED tax credit permanent (eliminating any sunset date).

Full Harmonization with Federal Post-December 15, 2024 Reforms: Effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Bill 2 aligned the BC SR&ED tax credit directly with the federal SR&ED reforms:

10% Refundable Credit Expanded to ECPCs and Doubled to a $6 Million Expenditure Limit: Both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) may claim a 10% refundable tax credit on the lesser of their SR&ED qualified BC expenditure for the tax year or their federal expenditure limit—which is increased from $3 million to $6,000,000 (doubling the maximum annual refundable BC credit from $300,000 to $600,000).

Expanded $15M–$75M Phase-Out Range: Because BC adopts the federal expenditure limit under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the federal ITA, the $6 million BC refundable limit phases out over the broader $15 million to $75 million prior-year taxable capital (or 3-year average revenue) range.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures: BC restored the eligibility of post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures as BC qualified expenditures.

10% Non-Refundable Credit and Filing Rules: All qualifying corporations (including non-CCPC/ECPCs, active members of partnerships, and CCPCs/ECPCs with BC qualified expenditures exceeding their refundable credit) can claim a 10% non-refundable tax credit against BC income tax payable (less any refundable credit claimed or amount renounced), with a 3-year carryback and 10-year carryforward. Claims on Form T666 must be filed no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the qualified expenditures were incurred.

body.text: 7.4 Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — 8% Base and 20% Incremental Tiers)

Effective January 1, 2021, Alberta established the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) under Division 7 of Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (detailed in Information Circular IEG-1R3), administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) using Form AT1 Schedule 29 (Alberta Innovation Employment Grant) and Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Claimed in Alberta):

items: Two-Tier Refundable Rate Structure (8% Base + 12% Incremental = 20% Total): The IEG is a refundable tax credit available to qualified corporations incurring eligible SR&ED expenditures in Alberta on up to a $4,000,000 Maximum Expenditure Limit per taxation year (shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years):

Part I Base Calculation (8% Rate): The corporation earns an 8% payment on the lesser of its eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures for the year (Line 031 of Schedule 29) and its Maximum Expenditure Limit (Line 108, up to $4,000,000).

Part II Incremental Calculation (+12% Additional Rate = 20% Total Rate): On the portion of its eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures (up to the $4,000,000 limit) that exceeds its Base Amount (or allocated allowed amount if associated), the corporation earns an additional 12% payment—bringing the total enhanced credit rate on spending above the Base Amount to 20% (8% + 12%).

Calculation of the Base Amount: For a non-associated corporation, the Base Amount (Line 118 of Schedule 29) is the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures for the two immediately preceding taxation years (for example, if eligible expenditures were $0 in Year 1 and $20,000 in Year 2, the Base Amount in Year 3 is [$0 + $20,000] ÷ 2 = $10,000).

Taxable Capital Phase-Out ($10M to $50M): The $4,000,000 Maximum Expenditure Limit phases out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (from Line 690 of federal Schedule T2SCH33) using the formula ($40,000,000 − [Line 126 − $10,000,000]) ÷ $40,000,000.

Current Expenditures Rule and Filing Deadline: As instructed on AT1 Schedule 29 (TRA14637), for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, Alberta IEG eligible expenditures use the federal amount of current SR&ED expenditures reported on Line 557 of federal Form T661. The filing deadline for AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 is 15 months after the corporation's filing due date, and payment follows CRA verification of the qualifying federal SR&ED claim.

body.text: 7.5 Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes: Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon
All six of the remaining provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA):

items: Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH380): Provides a 15% tax credit on eligible expenditures made after April 11, 2017 in Manitoba. For in-house R&D, half of the credit (7.5%) is refundable and the remainder (7.5%) is non-refundable. For eligible expenditures where R&D is carried out in Manitoba under a contract with a qualifying institute, the entire 15% credit is 100% fully refundable. Non-refundable tax credits can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years. The filing deadline is 1 year after the filing due date.

Saskatchewan Research and Development Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH403): Provides a 10% tax credit on eligible expenditures in Saskatchewan. For CCPCs (since April 1, 2017), the credit is a 10% refundable R&D tax credit up to an annual limit of $1,000,000 in eligible expenditures, and a 10% non-refundable R&D tax credit for expenditures in excess of $1,000,000. For all other corporations, the 10% tax credit is non-refundable. Non-refundable tax credits can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 10 years against Saskatchewan income taxes payable.

Nova Scotia Research and Development Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH340): Provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit on eligible expenditures in Nova Scotia, with a filing deadline of 18 months after the corporation's tax year-end.

New Brunswick Research and Development Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH360): Provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit on eligible expenditures incurred in New Brunswick. (Legacy non-refundable credits can be carried back 3 years and forward 7 years).

Newfoundland and Labrador Research and Development Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH301 for Corporations; Form T1129 for Individuals): Provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit on eligible expenditures in Newfoundland and Labrador, with a filing deadline of 12 months after the filing due date.

Yukon Research and Development Tax Credit: Provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit on eligible expenditures incurred in Yukon (available to corporations with a permanent establishment in Yukon, Yukon resident individuals, trust beneficiaries, and partnership members), plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.

body.text: 8. Governing Authorities, Pre-Claim Approval, Filing Procedures, and Audit Compliance
8.1 Institutional Roles of the Canada Revenue Agency, Department of Finance, Revenu Québec, and Alberta TRA
Administration of Canada's R&D tax incentives is divided across four primary governmental bodies:

items: Department of Finance Canada: Formulates statutory tax policy, drafts legislative amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations (such as Bill C-15 and the Budget 2025/2026 reforms), and approves prescribed special-purpose buildings on a building-by-building basis under ITR section 2903.

Canada Revenue Agency (CRA): Administers the federal SR&ED program and all provincial/territorial R&D tax credits except those of Québec and Alberta. Within the CRA's SR&ED program, claims are evaluated by two specialist groups: Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs)—who are guided by the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors to evaluate whether claimed work meets the definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1)—and Financial Reviewers—who are guided by the Financial Claim Review Manual – Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers to verify allowable expenditures, salary bases, specified employee caps, contract rules, and assistance reductions.

Revenu Québec (and Ministère des Finances du Québec): Administers the Québec Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (as well as legacy pre-March 26, 2025 R&D forms), relying on the CRA's scientific review for harmonized R&D work while administering pre-commercialization and Québec expenditure rules.

Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA): Administers the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) on Form AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970, issuing payments following CRA verification of the qualifying federal SR&ED claim.

body.text: 8.2 The Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322 and 90-Day Accelerated Review)

Introduced in the Canada Strong Budget 2025 and officially launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026, the SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval process allows businesses to have their planned work evaluated to ensure it meets SR&ED technical eligibility requirements before beginning their project and incurring significant costs (or when work has only recently begun).

To meet the eligibility criteria for Pre-Claim Approval, a business must operate in Canada as a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC), another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership, have an annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and be in good standing with the CRA. Furthermore, each submitted project must address a scientific or technological uncertainty through a systematic investigation, must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim, and must not involve issues currently under objection or in litigation.
The four-step Pre-Claim Approval application workflow operates as follows:

items: Request a Case Number: The claimant completes a short web form on Canada.ca; existing SR&ED claimants receive a case number in My Business Account within 2 business days, while new SR&ED claimants receive a phone call and case number from the CRA within 5 business days.

Complete and Upload Form T1322: The claimant completes Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) pre-claim approval), requesting pre-claim approval for up to 3 projects (entering the 15-character Business Number on Line 012, total number of projects up to 3 on Line 014, case number on Line 016, project title on Line 020, anticipated project start date on Line 022, estimated total SR&ED expenditures on Line 024, field of science or technology code on Line 026, technical descriptions of uncertainty, hypotheses, and planned experiments in Section B, preparer details on Lines 050–060, and authorization signature and date on Lines 080–082) and uploads Form T1322 plus up to 10 supporting documents via My Business Account under "Submit documents".

Meet with a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) Within 4 Weeks: Within four weeks of submitting the completed application, the CRA assigns an RTA for a 2-to-5-hour meeting (mandatory for new SR&ED claimants; optional at the RTA's request for existing SR&ED claimants in good standing) to discuss the existing state of knowledge or technology, the scientific or technological uncertainty, the work to be carried out, and how the systematic investigation or search will be structured.

Receive Official Determination Within 8 Weeks: Within 8 weeks of submitting a completed application in My Business Account, the CRA provides a formal Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report confirming whether pre-claim approval is granted and providing a detailed rationale and recommendations.

body.text: If granted, Pre-Claim Approval is valid for up to 3 years (and is reported on updated Lines 212 and 214 of Form T661 when the annual SR&ED claim is filed). Applying for Pre-Claim Approval is optional, and the CRA does not assess expenditures during the pre-claim stage; businesses must still submit a formal SR&ED claim after undertaking the work. Crucially, for SR&ED claims containing only projects that were granted Pre-Claim Approval and that are selected for an expenditure review, the CRA's processing time is cut in half from 180 days to 90 days.
8.3 Prescribed Forms, Line-by-Line Form T661 Architecture, and the Absolute 18-Month Reporting Deadline
A. Architecture of Prescribed Form T661 (Updated May 2026)

To claim federal SR&ED incentives, every claimant must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, governed by Guide T4088) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals and trusts). Form T661 is organized into ten parts:

items: Part 1 (Lines 010–157) — General Information: Claimant name (Line 010), tax year dates, 15-character Business Number, total number of projects (Line 050), financial contact (Lines 100–110), technical contact (Lines 115–125), and partnership details (Lines 151–157).

Part 2 (Lines 200–282) — Project Information: Must be prepared for every project claimed; claimants may choose to submit Part 2 for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value at the time of filing, but must complete and maintain Part 2 at their place of business for every project claimed and provide them upon CRA request, or face complete disallowance of the expenditures for those projects. Part 2 includes Project title (Line 200), start date (Line 202), completion or expected completion date (Line 204), field of science/technology code and CRDC research code (Lines 206–207), project claim history (Lines 208–210), Pre-Claim Approval fields (Lines 212–214), joint/collaborative work (Lines 218–221), and Section B Technical Narratives (each subject to a strict 350-word maximum): Line 242 (What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome?), Line 244 (What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the technological obstacles/uncertainties described in Line 242?), and Line 246 (What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve or attempt to achieve as a result of the work described in Line 244?). Part 2 also captures project preparer information (Lines 253–259), up to three key directly involved individuals and their qualifications (Lines 260–261), Lines 262–263 (the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024 and their SR&ED operating time percentages), external contractors (Lines 265–269), and the Contemporaneous Evidence Checklist (Lines 270–282).

Part 3 (Lines 160–162 & Lines 300–470) — Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures: Overhead method selection (Line 160 Proxy vs. Line 162 Traditional), allowable SR&ED expenditures (Lines 300–400, including Line 390 for post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures), and Section C calculation of the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Lines 429–470).

Part 4 (Lines 500–570) — Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes: Additions for prior-year unpaid amounts paid (Line 500), PPA (Line 502), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and NAL transfers in (Line 508), less reductions for assistance/contract payments (Lines 513–517, 538), unpaid amounts at 180 days (Line 520), 20% of arm's length contracts and third-party payments (Line 529), prescribed expenditures and pre-December 16, 2024 capital property (Lines 530, 535), 100% of NAL contracts (Line 541), NAL supplier cost adjustments (Line 542), and NAL transfers out (Line 544), plus repayments of assistance (Line 560) to yield Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures on Line 570.

Part 5 (Lines 810–820) — Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA): Salary base calculation for non-specified employees (Line 810) and specified employees, 55% PPA calculation (Line 820), and Overall PPA Cap.
Parts 6 to 10: Project costs for all projects claimed (Part 6), additional information (Part 7), claim checklist (Part 8), Claim Preparer Information (Part 9), and Certification (Part 10).

body.text: B. The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline

Under subsections 37(11) and 37(11.1) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, a claimant's SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred:

items: Corporations: Because a corporation's T2 filing due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporation's statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of its taxation year. (Exception: A non-profit SR&ED corporation has up to 6 months after the end of its tax year to file Form T661 under paragraph 149(1)(j) and cannot claim an ITC).

Individuals (Sole Proprietors): Because an individual's T1 filing due date is April 30 of the following year (or June 15 if the individual or their spouse/common-law partner carried on a business), their SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after that filing due date (17.5 months after year-end, on June 15 of the second following year, for business filers).
Trusts: Because a trust's T3 filing due date is within 90 days after its taxation year-end, a trust's SR&ED reporting deadline is 15 months after the end of its taxation year.

Partnerships: Form T661 should be filed with the partnership information return (T5013) no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing due dates for the return of income of the members for the tax year in which the partnership's fiscal period ends, and individual partners claim ITCs on their respective returns based on the deadlines applicable to their taxpayer status.

body.text: Under subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA (enacted following Alex Parallel Computers Research Inc. v. Canada), the SR&ED reporting deadline cannot be extended. If Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND) containing the prescribed information are filed after the SR&ED reporting deadline, the expenditures are statutorily denied and no ITC is allowed (as strictly enforced in Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA, and Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 FCA).
8.4 Claim Preparer Disclosures (Part 9 Penalty) and Gross Negligence / Third-Party Civil Penalties
To deter non-compliant or overstated SR&ED claims, the ITA and CRA enforce three categories of statutory penalties:

items: Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty ($1,000): Part 9 of Form T661 requires prescribed information for each claim preparer that has accepted consideration to prepare or assist in the preparation of the SR&ED claim, including billing arrangements. If the prescribed information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, the SR&ED claim will not be disallowed, but a $1,000 penalty may be assessed for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable (note: Part 9 information is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline).

Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2) of the ITA): Governed by the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), subsection 163(2) applies penalties where a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes a false statement or omission in an SR&ED claim (and misrepresentations also permit the CRA to reopen statute-barred taxation years, as occurred in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173, where supplier/website text was plagiarized in technical reports).

Third-Party Civil Penalties (Section 163.2 of the ITA) and Fraud Fines: Third-party civil penalties for preparers and advisors are provided for in section 163.2 of the ITA. Furthermore, judicial proceedings for SR&ED fraud involving false dates or false representations have resulted in court-imposed fines ranging from 150% to 300% of the amount claimed (e.g., R. v. Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684, and Tempora, SCC 2018).

body.text: 8.5 CRA Technical (RTA) and Financial Review Procedures and Contemporaneous Documentation Standards

Guided by The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025), the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, the Financial Claim Review Manual – Review Procedures for Financial Reviewers, and the Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns, CRA reviews evaluate both technical eligibility and financial compliance:

items: The Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) evaluates whether the claimed work meets the "Why" and "How" requirements of subsection 248(1) by interviewing the technical personnel who performed or supervised the work (listed on Line 260 of Form T661) and examining the contemporaneous supporting evidence indicated on Lines 270–282 (project planning documents, design of experiments, CAD/technical drawings, lab notebooks, software architecture and source code, trial run records, progress reports, meeting minutes, test protocols/data/results, analysis/conclusions, photographs/videos, prototypes/samples, and scrap records).

The Financial Reviewer verifies how claimed expenditures link to the eligible work, auditing T4 payroll records, time sheets/resource allocation records, arm's length and non-arm's length contracts, material consumption/transformation records, post-December 15, 2024 capital property and Shared-Use Equipment operating-time records, and government/non-government assistance reductions.

body.text: 9. Landmark Canadian Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents (1988–2026)
9.1 Foundational Appellate and Tax Court Precedents on Technological Eligibility
Canadian SR&ED law is shaped by a rigorous body of jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA):

items: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC): The foundational decision in Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence. Justice Bowman evaluated five hydraulic model engineering projects and held four of the five eligible, articulating the five-part test for SR&ED: (1) technical risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; (2) formulation of hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty via a five-stage process (observation of the problem, clear objective, articulation of uncertainty, formulation of hypotheses, and methodical testing); (3) procedures according with the total discipline of the scientific method; (4) resulting technological advancement in general understanding available to knowledgeable persons in the field; and (5) detailed records of hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed. Justice Bowman established that system uncertainty qualifies even when known components are used, that routine engineering refers to techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, that hindsight bias must be avoided because what appears obvious after the event may not have been obvious before the work was undertaken, and that the rejection of a hypothesis after testing is nonetheless a technological advance.

RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132 (FCA): The Federal Court of Appeal formally adopted Justice Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic analytical framework (allowing the taxpayer's appeal where a key engineer witness had died prior to trial, while emphasizing that systematic investigation requires documented evidence of testing and analysis beyond merely producing a new product or patent).

CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 284 N.R. 386 (FCA): Reaffirmed and summarized Justice Bowman's five questions as the governing appellate standard for determining whether activities constitute SR&ED.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Canada, 2011 FCA 355 (aff'g 2011 TCC 261): Confirmed that the five Northwest Hydraulic / CW Agencies questions apply to determine eligibility under subsection 248(1).

1726437 Ontario Inc. (o/a AirMax Technologies) v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376: Articulated the "catch and release" concept of subsection 248(1) and allowed HVAC system-uncertainty claims involving heat-source pressure ducts.

Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205: Held at paragraph 37 that the five-factor test is strictly cumulative: "To be eligible for SR&ED, each of the questions in the five-factor test must be answered in the affirmative." If any single criterion fails, the activities fail to qualify as SR&ED.

Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88: Clarified that although the specific words "scientific method" do not appear verbatim in subsection 248(1), Justice Bowman was interpreting the core statutory definition of SR&ED based on a textual, contextual, and purposive analysis when formulating the five-factor test.

National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47): In a unanimous decision written by Rennie J.A., the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed a software claimant's appeal and established three major legal principles: (1) CRA administrative policy guidelines (including the 2015 and 2021 guidelines and the "Why/How" framework) are non-binding on courts and do not supersede Northwest Hydraulic; (2) the scientific method requirement applies to applied sciences and software development within the context of the taxpayer's business environment; and (3) a proposed expert witness report is inadmissible under Rule 145 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) and White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co. (2015 SCC 23) where the claimant wrote 65% of the report and the report acted as legal advocacy rather than independent expert opinion.

body.text: 9.2 Software, Information Technology, and Systems Engineering Jurisprudence
Software and IT claims have generated nuanced Tax Court jurisprudence distinguishing routine software engineering from eligible SR&ED:

items: ACSIS EHR (Electronic Health Record) Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 263 (and 2016 TCC 50): Allowed software SR&ED claims where developers worked to increase system stability and no existing methods were available.
CRL Engineering Ltd. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 65: Allowed distributed computing claims involving sequentially progressive complex options investigated by a PhD researcher.

Indusol Industrial Control Ltd. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 103: Disallowed marine control software and system integration claims because the work did no more than identify problems without a systematic experimental investigation.
Allegro Wireless Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 27: Allowed all three claimed telecommunications and AI/software projects.

DAZZM Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129: A pivotal software victory in which the Tax Court allowed claims involving cloud-based SaaS integration and React/Redux performance optimization, holding that systemic uncertainty in open-source tool integration went beyond routine debugging or optimization, and reinforcing documentation through metrics and witness testimony.
Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7: Issued in 2026, this split decision illustrates the boundary for industrial control software:
Allowed Project (MTCLM): Developing a SIL 4 train-control box involved cumulative "system uncertainty" not resolvable by available methods.
Disallowed Project (SCADACOM-5 — $1,293,692 disallowed): Modernization and scale-up of a SCADA system using known tools was held to be commercial product development, not experimental development.

body.text: 9.3 Manufacturing, Process Engineering, Energy, and Agricultural Jurisprudence

items: Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. (1988 TCC): Early manufacturing precedent on technological eligibility and systematic testing.

Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313: Held across four process projects with sparse written records that highly credible verbal evidence from technical witnesses can establish SR&ED eligibility.

Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6: Disallowed theatrical rigging claims, reiterating that uncertainty must be a type that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures.

Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42 and Béton Mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 278: Clarified that the required knowledge must genuinely not exist in the base of scientific or technological knowledge available to competent professionals, rather than simply being unknown to the claimant due to a lack of knowledge transfer or personal inexperience.
Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18: Allowed tractor design claims, illustrating how system integration uncertainties satisfy the Northwest Hydraulic test.

Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2023 TCC 35: Disallowed jewellery design and manufacturing claims for failing to demonstrate knowledge beyond that apparent to a BSc in the field or adherence to the five-factor test.

Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63, Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC), and Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 183: Three 2025 Tax Court decisions that rejected claims based on trial-and-error prototyping, vague or reconstructed narratives, and unsubstantiated wage allocations split evenly across batches.

Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC): Allowed food-science SR&ED claims for developing a shelf-stable cold-pressed juice ("Chrisoda") using novel high-pressure processing (HPP) applications, holding that testing hypotheses through measurable observations (pH and microbial counts) validated systematic investigation.

body.text: 9.4 Jurisprudence on Financial Calculations, Government Assistance, CCPC Control, Deadlines, and Penalties

items: Fixed-Price Contracts vs. Contract Payments (Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen, 1999 TCC): Held that a fixed-price commercial contract where the taxpayer bears the risk is not a purchase of SR&ED on behalf of the customer, preserving the performer's ITCs.
Loans as Government Assistance (CAE Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA): Held that government loans related to R&D constitute government assistance that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Experimental Production Runs and Material Sales (Les Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. v. The Queen, 1992 TCC; Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 DTC 724 [1997 TCC]): Confirmed that SR&ED labour and materials required for experimental production remain eligible despite subsequent sale of the output (leading to legislative ITC recapture rules on materials sold).

Medical Professional Corporations (André Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 61): Held that SR&ED work performed by a doctor was deemed on behalf of his Medical Professional Corporation (MPC) across four eligible project examples.

De Facto Control and CCPC Status (HSC Research, 1995 TCC; McGillivray Restaurant Ltd., 2016 FCA; Aeronautic Development Corp., 2017 TCC 39; CO2 Solution Technologies, 2019 CCI 286): Established the factors for evaluating de facto control when determining CCPC qualification.

Strict 18-Month Filing Deadline (Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA / 2015 TCC 211; Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 FCA / 2017 TCC 9): Confirmed that the 18-month deadline is absolute and that all prescribed information must be filed in prescribed form (including Schedule T2SCH31) by the deadline.

Plagiarized Narratives and Gross Negligence Penalties (Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173): While allowing certain 2007–2008 heating-element projects, the Tax Court denied the 2006 and 2009 claims and held that plagiarized supplier/website text in technical reports constituted a misrepresentation that reopened statute-barred years and supported section 163(2) penalties.
